facts.raw_span: A 37-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus and Sjögren’s syndrome
was diagnosed with autoimmune hepatitis
Vital signs and physical examination were unremarkable
Antrum: normal appearance
Gastric corpus: normal coloration with a regular arrangement of collecting venules; red streaks and slight mucosal swelling on the lesser curvature of the angle
Magnified narrow-band imaging of the corpus: regular round pit patterns
Three defined layers: first (foveolar epithelium) showed foveolar hyperplasia
second (parietal cells) was shortened with mild degeneration
H+/K+-ATPase staining: heterogeneously reduced
Anti-parietal cell antibody: <1:10 (negative)
Serum gastrin: 150 pg/mL (normal 37–172)
Anti-H. pylori IgG: <3 U/mL (negative)

concepts.why: The patient's gastric corpus shows foveolar hyperplasia, shortened parietal cells with mild degeneration, and heterogeneously reduced H+/K+-ATPase staining, which are characteristic of autoimmune gastritis.
The patient was diagnosed with autoimmune hepatitis, and the presence of autoimmune gastritis and Sjögren's syndrome suggests a broader autoimmune disorder.
The patient has Sjögren's syndrome, which is an autoimmune disorder that can cause various systemic symptoms.
The patient has systemic lupus erythematosus, which is a chronic autoimmune disorder that can affect multiple organ systems.
The patient's gastric corpus shows red streaks, slight mucosal swelling, and mild lymphocytic infiltration, which are indicative of gastric mucosal inflammation.
The patient's gastric corpus shows atrophy of the parietal cells and heterogeneously reduced H+/K+-ATPase staining, which are characteristic of atrophic gastritis.
The patient has a negative anti-parietal cell antibody test, but the presence of atrophic gastritis and autoimmune disorders increases the risk of pernicious anemia.
The patient's gastric corpus shows foveolar hyperplasia and mild lymphocytic infiltration, which can be indicative of gastric metaplasia.
It explains the finding of red streaks and slight mucosal swelling on the lesser curvature of the angle in the gastric corpus.

rationales.F01: Systemic lupus erythematosus is associated with various autoimmune conditions, including Sjögren's syndrome, which may increase the likelihood of autoimmune gastritis.
rationales.F02: Autoimmune hepatitis is a distinct condition that may not directly relate to gastric conditions, but its presence in a patient with other autoimmune diseases may suggest a higher likelihood of autoimmune gastritis.
rationales.F08: Mild degeneration of parietal cells is a characteristic finding in autoimmune gastritis, which supports the diagnosis.
rationales.F09: Heterogeneously reduced H+/K+-ATPase staining is indicative of parietal cell dysfunction, which is consistent with autoimmune gastritis.
rationales.F10: The absence of anti-parietal cell antibodies makes autoimmune gastritis less likely, but it does not rule out the condition entirely.

frontier_selector.rationale: The patient's histologic findings, including foveolar hyperplasia, shortened parietal cells with mild degeneration, and heterogeneously reduced H+/K+-ATPase staining, are consistent with atrophic gastritis. While autoimmune gastritis is also a possible diagnosis, the lack of positive anti-parietal cell antibodies and the presence of mild lymphocytic infiltration suggest atrophic gastritis as a more specific diagnosis.
